content: Congenital heart disease (ConHD) affects approximately 1% of all live births. Advances in medical care have significantly improved survival rates for individuals with ConHD, but these individuals remain at an elevated risk of developing non-communicable diseases. Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) is notably reduced in people with ConHD, and their physical fitness tends to decline more rapidly compared to healthy individuals. CRF is a well-established predictor of future mortality and morbidity, making it critical to evaluate the evidence surrounding physical activity interventions in this population to guide clinical decision-making. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of various physical activity interventions compared to standard care in individuals with ConHD. A systematic search was conducted on September 23, 2019, across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and others. ClinicalTrials.gov was also searched, and reference lists of relevant systematic reviews were examined. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing any type of physical activity intervention to a control group receiving no physical activity (usual care) were included. Participants of all ages with a diagnosis of ConHD, regardless of prior medical interventions, were eligible for inclusion. Two independent reviewers screened the identified studies, retrieved full-text articles, and contacted study authors for additional information when necessary. Data extraction and risk of bias assessment were performed independently by the same reviewers using the RoB 2 tool. The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Primary outcomes included maximal CRF (measured by peak oxygen consumption), health-related quality of life (HRQoL) assessed via validated questionnaires, and objective measures of physical activity using wearable devices. The review included 15 RCTs with a total of 924 participants. The median duration of interventions or follow-up was 12 weeks, with an interquartile range of 12 to 26 weeks. Five studies focused on children and adolescents (n = 500), while 10 studies involved adults (n = 424). Three types of interventions were identified: physical activity promotion, exercise training, and inspiratory muscle training. The risk of bias for CRF outcomes was assessed as some concern in 12 studies and high risk in two studies, primarily due to the inability to blind intervention staff. One study did not report CRF outcomes. Using the GRADE approach, the certainty of evidence ranged from moderate to very low across the measured outcomes. When pooling all types of interventions (physical activity promotion, exercise training, and inspiratory muscle training) and comparing them to a no-exercise control, CRF showed a slight increase, with a mean difference (MD) of 1.89 mL/kg/min (95% CI: -0.22 to 3.99; n = 732; moderate-certainty evidence). The effect of physical activity and exercise interventions on HRQoL was highly uncertain, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.76 (95% CI: -0.13 to 1.65; n = 163; very low-certainty evidence). Only three studies could be pooled for HRQoL analysis due to variability in reporting methods, and only one of these studies demonstrated a positive effect on HRQoL. Physical activity interventions may lead to a small improvement in mean daily physical activity levels, with an SMD of 0.38 (95% CI: -0.15 to 0.92; n = 328; low-certainty evidence), equivalent to approximately 10 additional minutes of daily physical activity (95% CI: -2.50 to 22.20 minutes). Submaximal CRF, assessed at the gas exchange threshold, likely increased with physical activity and exercise interventions, with an MD of 2.05 mL/kg/min (95% CI: 0.05 to 4.05; n = 179; moderate-certainty evidence). Muscular strength, measured by maximal voluntary contraction of knee extensions, also likely improved, with an MD of 17.13 (95% CI: 3.45 to 30.81; n = 18; moderate-certainty evidence). Adverse events were reported in 11 studies (n = 501), accounting for 73% of the included studies. Six studies reported no adverse events, while five studies documented a total of 11 adverse events, 36% of which were cardiac-related (n = 4). Importantly, no serious adverse events or fatalities related to the interventions were reported (moderate-certainty evidence). None of the studies reported on hospital admissions. In conclusion, this review provides an overview of the current evidence on the effects of physical activity interventions on CRF, HRQoL, and physical activity levels in individuals with ConHD. While small improvements in CRF and physical activity levels were observed, and no serious adverse events were reported, the evidence remains insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the impact of these interventions. Further high-quality RCTs with longer follow-up durations are needed to better understand the potential benefits and risks of physical activity interventions in this population.
